issues.legal_issue: A tax liability deductible from compensation affects the compensation right’s market value when deduction remains possible, but is not separately deducted from net wealth.
material_facts: The estate had vested in the State, and compensation was payable to the assessee under the land-reform scheme.
Agricultural income tax was due from the assessee and was deductible from the compensation under the scheme if it had not already been deducted before issue of the compensation bond.
issues.conclusion: The agricultural income tax arrears were not to be deducted separately from net wealth. If they had not already been deducted, the possibility and hazard of their deduction had to be considered in valuing the compensation right.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 7 and 2(m) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, asset valuation and deduction of debts operate at different stages, but section 7(1) requires valuation by reference to market value and relevant hazards. A liability deductible from compensation is a factor a willing purchaser would consider. The Court followed Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Bihar, Patna v. Maharaja Kumar Kamal Singh, Civil Appeal Nos. 1238 to 1240 (NT) of 1973.

rule.if: wealth_tax_valuation_case and compensation_right_is_an_asset and tax_liability_is_deductible_from_compensation and deduction_not_already_made

predicates.wealth_tax_valuation_case: The proceeding concerns valuation of a taxpayer’s wealth for wealth tax purposes.
predicates.compensation_right_is_an_asset: The taxpayer holds a right to receive compensation that is included among the assets being valued.
predicates.tax_liability_is_deductible_from_compens: A tax liability of the taxpayer may be deducted from the compensation payable.
predicates.deduction_not_already_made: The possible deduction has not already been made from the compensation before its valuation.

issues.definition: When the proceeding values a compensation right as an asset and an outstanding tax liability may be deducted from it, the possibility of that deduction is treated as a hazard affecting the right’s value.

issues.legal_issue: An unexecuted money decree must be valued by estimating its open-market price in light of realization risks, rather than automatically at its face amount or at nil because of an attachment.
material_facts: The assessee held two civil-court money decrees that remained unexecuted and were shown at their full amounts in his books.
A garnishee order concerning one decree had been issued to secure the assessee’s liability to a bank; another attachment order was issued after the relevant valuation dates.
The tax authority valued the decrees at their full amounts, while the assessee argued that an attached decree had no value.
issues.conclusion: The decrees had to be valued under section 7(1) by estimating what a willing purchaser would pay in the open market on the valuation date, taking account of the hazards of execution and realization. Their book amounts did not establish their market value, and attachment did not by itself make a decree valueless.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(1) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957 requires estimation of an asset’s market value. A pending decree is an asset, but its value depends on what a willing purchaser would pay after considering realization hazards; the fact that the decree is recorded at face value in the taxpayer’s books is not conclusive. The Court relied on Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Bihar, Patna v. Maharaja Kumar Kamal Singh, Civil Appeal Nos. 1238 to 1240 (NT) of 1973, and held that section 7(2)(a) had not been used to value these decrees.

rule.if: wealth_tax_valuation_case and money_decree_is_an_asset and decree_remains_unexecuted and (execution_or_realization_risk_exists or garnishee_order_affects_recovery)

predicates.wealth_tax_valuation_case: The proceeding concerns valuation of a taxpayer’s wealth for wealth tax purposes.
predicates.money_decree_is_an_asset: The taxpayer holds a money decree that is included among the assets being valued.
predicates.decree_remains_unexecuted: The decree has not yet been executed.
predicates.execution_or_realization_risk_exists: There are uncertainties or hazards in executing the decree or realizing its proceeds.
predicates.garnishee_order_affects_recovery: A court order attaches or otherwise affects recovery of the amount due under the decree.

issues.definition: An unexecuted decree in a wealth tax valuation is valued by its likely open-market price when execution or recovery is uncertain or affected by attachment.

issues.legal_issue: A claim decree against a debtor is an asset whose value depends on what a reasonable purchaser would pay after considering the debtor’s ability to satisfy it and other realization hazards.
material_facts: The assessee held claim decrees against several debtors.
The High Court found that one claim decree could be satisfied wholly or partly only from compensation payable to the debtor under the land-reform scheme.
The tax authorities had valued the claim decrees, and the High Court directed that they be valued by estimating their open-market price with all hazards considered.
issues.conclusion: The claim decrees were assets, but they had to be valued by estimating what a reasonable person would pay for them on the valuation date, taking into account the source and likelihood of recovery and all other hazards.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(1) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957 requires valuation of an asset by its market value. For a claim decree, that requires estimating what a reasonable person would pay in the open market while considering the means by which the debtor can satisfy the decree and other realization hazards. The Court relied on Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Bihar, Patna v. Maharaja Kumar Kamal Singh, Civil Appeal Nos. 1238 to 1240 (NT) of 1973.

predicates.wealth_tax_valuation_case: The proceeding concerns valuation of a taxpayer’s wealth for wealth tax purposes.
predicates.taxpayer_holds_claim_decree: The taxpayer holds a decree establishing a claim against a debtor.
predicates.recovery_depends_on_debtor_assets_or_com: Satisfaction of the decree depends wholly or partly on assets or compensation available to the debtor.

issues.definition: A claim decree is valued by its likely open-market recovery when its satisfaction depends on the debtor’s available assets or compensation.

issues.legal_issue: Net wealth is calculated by valuing each asset and each debt separately, while considering in an asset’s market valuation any liability or hazard that would influence a prospective purchaser.
material_facts: The assessment included the assessee’s compensation rights and decrees as assets and considered debts owed by the assessee.
The revenue argued that each asset and debt should be separately valued and that a liability relating to an asset should be ignored when valuing that asset.

The Court accepted separate valuation and subtraction of aggregate debts from aggregate asset values, but rejected the proposition that relevant deduction hazards must be ignored when valuing an asset.
issues.conclusion: Each asset and each debt must be valued separately, and net wealth is the difference between their aggregate values. However, an asset’s market value must take account of a liability or possible deduction that would influence a prospective purchaser.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 7 and 2(m) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957 apply at different stages: section 7 governs estimation of asset market value, and section 2(m) provides for deduction of debts. The provisions operate harmoniously, so debts are accounted for separately while relevant hazards, including possible deductions from an asset, may affect that asset’s value. The Court relied on Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Bihar, Patna v. Maharaja Kumar Kamal Singh, Civil Appeal Nos. 1238 to 1240 (NT) of 1973.

predicates.wealth_tax_valuation_case: The proceeding concerns valuation of a taxpayer’s wealth for wealth tax purposes.
predicates.taxpayer_has_assets_and_debts: The taxpayer has assets to be valued and debts to be accounted for in calculating net wealth.

issues.definition: In a wealth tax valuation, net wealth uses separately valued assets and debts, while the market value of an asset reflects hazards that would affect what a purchaser would pay.

issues.legal_issue: A valuation finding by the tax tribunal does not bind the High Court when the tribunal reached it by applying incorrect principles.
material_facts: The tribunal determined values for the assessee’s assets.
The High Court considered whether the tribunal had applied the proper valuation principles.
The Supreme Court stated that although market value is a question of fact, a finding reached by taking wrong principles into account does not bind the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court may interfere with a tribunal’s valuation finding if it was reached by applying wrong principles; a factual valuation finding is not binding in that circumstance.
issues.legal_principle: Market value is ordinarily a question of fact for the tax tribunal, but a finding reached by applying wrong principles does not bind the High Court. The Court applied section 7(1) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957 as the governing valuation provision; no earlier case was cited for this specific statement about review of the tribunal’s finding.

predicates.wealth_tax_reference_proceeding: The proceeding is a reference to a High Court concerning a wealth tax assessment.
predicates.tribunal_made_asset_valuation_finding: The tax tribunal made a factual finding about the value of an asset.
predicates.tribunal_applied_wrong_valuation_princip: The tribunal reached its valuation finding by applying incorrect principles.

issues.definition: In a wealth tax reference, the High Court may disregard the tribunal’s asset valuation finding when the tribunal applied incorrect valuation principles.
